questions.q: The Task API sends a reminder email while the user waits. Which set of problems does a job queue fix?
questions.explain: The request only writes down a job and answers at once. A worker does the work later, retries failures, and parks jobs that never succeed where a person can see them.
options: The email looks ugly, uses too much memory, and has no subject
The request is slow, it fails when the mail server is down, and a crash can lose the email without anyone knowing
The user cannot log in, the database is locked, and the cache is stale
Emails cannot be sent from Node.js at all

questions.q: A route adds a reminder job and answers straight away. Which status code fits best?
questions.explain: 202 Accepted means "I have your request and will do it", not "it is done". The work happens after the response.
options: 200 OK with the sent email
201 Created
202 Accepted
204 No Content

questions.q: Which of these should not become a background job?
questions.explain: The user needs the login answer right now, and it is fast, so it is a direct call. Slow or unreliable work that the user does not wait for belongs on a queue.
options: Generating a 200-page PDF export
Calling a partner's webhook that is often slow
Checking a password at login
Resizing an uploaded image

questions.q: What should a reminder job's data contain?
questions.explain: Queues are stored, logged and shown in dashboards, so never put secrets in a job. Whole objects may have changed by the time the job runs, so pass ids and load fresh data.
options: The whole task object and the SMTP password, so the processor has everything
Small, plain data like the task id; the processor loads fresh data by id and reads secrets from its own configuration
The user's session cookie, so the processor can act as the user
Nothing at all; jobs cannot carry data

questions.q: Why not set a queue's concurrency to 1,000?
questions.explain: Pick a number that the slowest thing your jobs touch can handle, for example the 10 connections a mail provider allows or a database pool of 20.
options: Because JavaScript can only run one job at a time
Every running job uses memory and connections, and the service at the other end has limits too
Because higher concurrency makes each job slower to start
Because concurrency must always be 1

questions.q: Why use exponential backoff instead of retrying at once?
questions.explain: The waits double after each failure (1 s, 2 s, 4 s...) up to maxDelay. Retrying at once mostly hits the same outage again.
options: It makes every retry faster
A server that is down now is probably still down 1 ms later; doubling the wait gives a struggling service more and more room to recover
It stops retries completely after the first failure
It guarantees the job runs exactly once

questions.q: 5,000 jobs failed at the same moment. Why does jitter matter for their retries?
questions.explain: Jitter adds randomness to each wait. The default "full" picks a random wait between 0 and the computed one. Leave it on in production; turn it off only for predictable examples.
options: It makes the retries run in the order they were added
Without it, all 5,000 retry at the same moment too and knock the server over again; jitter spreads them out
It removes the backoff delay
It only matters in tests

questions.q: A processor sent the email and then failed while writing "sent" to the database. The job is retried. What happens, and what is the fix?
questions.explain: A retry runs the whole processor again. An idempotent processor is safe to run twice: it checks, for example, task.reminded before sending.
options: Nothing, the queue knows the email was already sent
The email is sent again; queues run jobs at least once, so make the processor idempotent (check whether the work was already done)
The job goes straight to the dead-letter queue
The queue undoes the email

questions.q: A job runs for the first time. What is job.attempt?
questions.explain: job.attempt counts the tries that came before this one, so it starts at 0. Add 1 if you want to print "try 1".
options: 1
0
undefined
The number of attempts allowed

questions.q: You add a job without an attempts option, and the processor throws. What happens?
questions.explain: attempts is the total number of tries, and the default is 1. Set it (and a backoff) for work that can fail temporarily, or set defaultJobOptions on the queue so no route forgets it.
options: It is retried forever
It is retried 3 times
The default is 1 attempt, which means no retry: the job goes to the dead-letter queue
The error is ignored and the job counts as completed

questions.q: You need a report built every night at 2:00. What does the lesson say?
questions.explain: delay and scheduledAt postpone one job. Repeating work is the scheduler's job, covered in the next lesson.
options: Add one job with delay: 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 and it repeats
A queue runs each job once; repeating work belongs to a scheduler, which adds a job at the right times
Use priority: CRITICAL so it runs every night
Use a while (true) loop inside the processor

questions.q: Jobs are piling up in the dead-letter queue. What is the most important thing to have in place?
questions.explain: Watch the count, find the cause, fix it, and replay the jobs with queue.add(dead.job.name, dead.job.data) when a bug caused the failures.
options: A job that deletes dead letters every night
An alert when the count grows: a dead-letter queue nobody looks at is just a slower way to lose data
A higher concurrency
Nothing, dead letters fix themselves

questions.q: The error is "mailbox does not exist". What is the best way to handle it in the processor?
questions.explain: Retries are for temporary failures. A permanent error only wastes retries. Record it so the user can fix their address, and keep throwing for errors that a retry can fix.
options: Throw it, so the queue retries 5 times with backoff
Give up at once: record the failure (for example in the database) and return normally, because retrying cannot help
Wait in a loop until the mailbox exists
Delete the user

questions.q: A job's timeout runs out. What must the processor do?
questions.explain: The queue aborts the signal and counts the attempt as failed, but it cannot stop a running function by force. A processor that ignores the signal keeps running in the background and wastes a slot.
options: Nothing, the queue kills the function at once
Watch context.signal (for example with throwIfAborted()) and stop itself
Call queue.close()
Increase the timeout from inside the job

questions.q: What does a graceful shutdown of a worker do?
questions.explain: Jobs that are simply cut off die halfway. worker.stop() waits for the running jobs; waiting jobs stay in the queue for the next worker.
options: Exits at once, so the new version starts faster
Stops taking new jobs, lets the running ones finish, and only then exits
Runs every waiting job before exiting
Moves all waiting jobs to the dead-letter queue

questions.q: Your platform kills a stopping process after 20 seconds. How should you set the worker's drainTimeout?
questions.explain: stop() waits at most drainTimeout (30 seconds by default) and then aborts the jobs still running. If the platform kills first, those jobs die without a clean stop.
options: Longer than 20 seconds, so jobs always finish
Shorter than 20 seconds, so stop() can abort the remaining jobs through their signal before the kill
Exactly 0, so nothing waits
It does not matter

questions.q: What is the main limit of createInMemoryQueue in production?
questions.explain: Production needs a queue backed by a shared store that survives restarts, such as Redis or PostgreSQL, behind the same Queue interface, so your processors do not change.
options: It cannot retry jobs
Jobs live in the process's memory: a restart loses every waiting job, and two copies of the API have two separate queues
It only runs in the browser
It cannot run jobs concurrently

questions.q: A user double-clicks "remind me". The second add throws JobDuplicateError because of the deduplicationKey. What should the route answer?
questions.explain: The duplicate key stopped a second copy of the same job. From the user's point of view, the reminder is queued, so catch JobDuplicateError and answer 202.
options: 500, because an error was thrown
409 Conflict with the error details
202 anyway: the reminder is queued
It should add the job again without the key

questions.q: Why create the queue with autoProcess: false when you use a separate worker?
questions.explain: The worker gives you control: its own concurrency, start() and stop(). autoProcess: false leaves all processing to it.
options: So jobs are never processed
So the queue does not start running jobs itself before the worker exists
So jobs are processed twice, once by each
So the queue ignores concurrency

questions.explain: The deduplicationKey refuses a second job with the same key while the first one exists, so only one reminder is queued.

questions.explain: The signal was aborted at 60 ms, in the middle of page 2. The processor finished that page, saw the signal before page 3, and stopped. With one attempt allowed, the job went to the dead-letter queue.
options: pages: 10 state: completed
pages: 1 state: dead_letter

questions.explain: The processor is idempotent: it checks reminded before sending, so running the job a second time does no harm.
options:
mail to ada@example.com
mail to ada@example.com

mail to ada@example.com
nothing to do

questions.q: Register a processor for send-reminder jobs that prints reminder for task <taskId> to <email>, then add one job for task 1 and ada@example.com. The rest waits for the job and closes the queue.
questions.explain: queue.process(name, processor) registers the function for that job name, and queue.add(name, data) stores a job. Always close() the queue when the program stops.
questions.expected:
reminder for task 1 to ada@example.com
done

questions.q: The mail server fails twice before it works. Change the add call so the job gets 4 attempts with a fixed backoff of 5 ms (createFixedBackoff(5)).
questions.explain: With the default of 1 attempt, the first failure sends the job to the dead-letter queue. attempts is the total number of tries, and backoff sets the wait before each retry.

questions.q: Make the processor idempotent. Load the task by job.data.taskId. If it is missing or already reminded, print task <id>: nothing to do and return. Otherwise print mail to <email> and set reminded to true.
questions.explain: Queues run jobs at least once, so a processor must be safe to run twice. It loads fresh data by id and checks whether the work was already done.
questions.expected:
mail to ada@example.com
task 1: nothing to do
task 7: nothing to do

questions.q: Addresses ending in @example.invalid can never work. In the processor, push such an address to failedAddresses and return normally, so no retries are wasted. Other addresses are "sent" (just count them in sent).
questions.explain: Retrying a permanent error cannot help. Record it (in a real app, in the database so the user sees it) and return. Keep throwing for temporary errors so the queue retries them.

questions.q: Write exponentialDelay(retry, base, maxDelay) by hand, without jitter: base for retry 1, doubled for each later retry, but never more than maxDelay.
questions.explain: 2 ** (retry - 1) doubles the wait each time, and Math.min caps it. In production the queue also adds jitter so many failed jobs do not retry at the same moment.

questions.q: Write pickNext(jobs), which returns the label of the job that runs next: the highest priority first, and among equal priorities the one with the smallest added number. Do not change the jobs array.
questions.explain: That is the queue's rule: higher priority first, and first come, first served among equals. Looping over the array (or sorting a copy) leaves the original untouched.

questions.q: Write a queue middleware log that prints start <job name> before ctx.next() and end <job name> after it, even when the job throws. Pass it in the queue's middleware option.
questions.explain: finally runs whether the job worked or threw. Return the result of ctx.next(), and do not swallow the error, so the queue can still retry or dead-letter the job.
questions.expected:
start send-reminder
  sending
end send-reminder
start broken
end broken

questions.q: The job has a 60 ms timeout and each page takes 40 ms. Make the processor stop soon after the timeout by calling context.signal.throwIfAborted() before each page.
questions.explain: The queue aborts the signal when the timeout runs out, but it cannot stop the function by force. The check before each page lets the processor stop itself instead of building pages nobody will use.

questions.q: Create a worker named worker-1 for the queue with concurrency: 2 and pollInterval: 5, start it, and after the 15 ms wait stop it gracefully.
questions.explain: worker.stop() stops taking new jobs and waits for the running ones to finish. Job 3 was never started, so it is still waiting for the next worker.

questions.q: Finish postReminder(taskId). Add the job with deduplicationKey: "reminder.task-<id>". If add throws an error whose name is JobDuplicateError, still answer { status: 202, body: { queued: true } }; re-throw any other error.
questions.explain: The second click finds the job already queued, so the honest answer is still 202. Only one job exists. Any other error is a real problem and must not be hidden.

questions.q: A bug made every job fail, and the jobs are now dead letters. The bug is fixed (bugFixed = true). Replay them: for each entry of queue.getDeadLetterJobs(), add the job again with queue.add(dead.job.name, dead.job.data).
questions.explain: Each dead letter keeps the job's name and data, so nothing was lost. Fix the cause first, then replay; replaying before the fix only fills the dead-letter queue again.
questions.expected:
sent reminder for task 1
sent reminder for task 2
